introduction: In 1910, two years after the Young Turk revolution freed him from forty years’ confinement, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá left Haifa for Egypt. He was sixty-six and ill; he stayed about a year, mostly in Alexandria, before sailing for Europe, and returned to Egypt between and after his Western journeys. This guide gathers his letters from those months. They are frank about exhaustion and “nervous fever”, modest about purpose (“a change of air”), and aware that after so long a door had opened. Paul’s letters have the same mixture of infirmity, travel plans and “a great door … opened”. Egypt is also Joseph’s country, as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá remarks.
questions: What do these letters show about how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá regarded his own health and limits?
He went first to Egypt, quietly, and only later to the West. What does that order suggest?
Paul wrote that his imprisonment had furthered his cause. In what sense was that true of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá?

outside.why: Written in convalescence: the body could not endure. My strength is made perfect in weakness.
Extreme weakness. Paul to Timothy: use a little wine for thy stomach’s sake and thine often infirmities. Apostles too had bodies to be looked after.
Port Said, then Ismailia, in search of a climate. Come ye yourselves apart, and rest a while.
Often ill, yet the work did not stop. In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often.
On reaching Egypt, exhaustion and nervous fever took complete hold. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures; he restoreth my soul.
The journey was solely for a change of air. To every thing there is a season: a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
The invisible hand has opened the doors. A great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries.
I entered Egypt trusting in God. Get thee out of thy country, unto a land that I will shew thee.
Joy at the journey from the centre of imprisonment. The things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel.
“The land of Joseph of Canaan.” Joseph came to Egypt a prisoner: but the Lord was with Joseph.
Isaiah has a blessing for the country that the reading names with affection: blessed be Egypt my people.
From the prison land to Egypt. Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt.
In Egypt there was no opportunity for writing or speech. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold. Why might a teacher freed after forty years begin with silence?
